voiceover.text: Last time, we tracked one person's health along the continuum. Now imagine you had to make a decision for the whole country. You've got one hundred million dollars, and you can spend it on cancer treatment or on preventing road injuries. You're not allowed to ask anyone's opinion, only for numbers. Which numbers would you ask for? To answer that, you need the tools for measuring a whole population's health.

A doctor sees one patient at a time, and can say what's wrong with that person. But a health system has to answer questions about groups, and those can only be answered by counting. That's epidemiology: the study of the patterns and causes of health and disease across populations. It asks four questions, in order. What's happening? To whom? Is it changing? And why, and what works? In Australia, the main source is Australia's Health, from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

The first measure is mortality, which counts deaths. It's usually given as a rate per 100,000 people, because a count can't compare a small town with a city. Mortality is the most reliable measure we have, because every death must be registered by law. Its weakness is that it says nothing about anyone still alive. Infant mortality counts deaths before age one, per 1,000 live births. It reacts quickly to housing, nutrition and access to care, so it's one of the most sensitive signs of how well a whole population is living.

Morbidity is the illness, disease and injury carried by people who are alive. In a country like Australia, where many conditions are managed for decades rather than being quickly fatal, that's where most of the burden sits. But morbidity is harder to measure, because most illness data come from services, so an illness usually gets counted only when someone goes to a service, is diagnosed, and is recorded. Surveys fill some of the gap, but if you never walk in the door, you often don't appear in the data.

The last two measures are the ones most often confused. Incidence counts new cases in a period, like a year. Prevalence counts all the cases present at one time, new and old together. Think of a bath. Incidence is the tap, the flow of new cases coming in. Prevalence is the water level, how many cases are in the bath right now. And the drain is people leaving, because they recover or they die.

Everything follows from the picture. Influenza has a fast tap and a fast drain, so incidence is high, but prevalence stays low, because people recover within days. Type one diabetes has a slow tap and almost no drain, because it's lifelong, so prevalence climbs year after year. And here's the surprise. A new treatment that stops people dying, without curing them, narrows the drain. Prevalence goes up, even though nothing got worse. In a table it looks like failure. It's actually success.

When you meet a table or graph you've never seen, ask five questions, in order. What's the unit, a count, a percentage, or a rate, and per how many? Who's in it, which ages, which years? Is it age-standardised? Which way is it moving? And what's missing? Age standardising matters more than it sounds. An area full of retirees will show far more cancer than a university suburb, just because its people are older. Standardising adjusts for age, so you're comparing health, not birthdays.

Now read three measures together. Here's a constructed table for one condition, in a population of two hundred thousand. New cases fall each year, so prevention is working. Deaths halve, so treatment is working. And prevalence rises by about a quarter. On its own, that rise looks like a worsening epidemic. But read with the other two columns, it's the result of the success. People who would have died are alive, and still counted. No single measure describes health status. You need them together.

These numbers are powerful, but they hide things. An average hides the spread, so a national figure can improve while one group gets worse. Morbidity data depends on being counted, so people who can't reach a service can look healthier than they are, which is exactly backwards. These measures count disease, not wellbeing, so they miss the mental and social dimensions. And the numbers arrive late, so reports describe the past.
Two things to remember. The bathtub: incidence is the tap, prevalence is the water level, and the drain is recovery or death. And prevalence can rise because mortality fell.

Two exam questions. First. In a town of fifty thousand people, one hundred and fifty people are newly diagnosed with a condition during one year, and twelve hundred people are living with it at the end of that year. Identify the incidence and the prevalence, and express the incidence as a rate per one hundred thousand people. Pause here to answer.

The one hundred and fifty new cases are the incidence, and the twelve hundred living with it are the prevalence. For the rate: one hundred and fifty, divided by fifty thousand, times one hundred thousand, which is three hundred per one hundred thousand. The classic slip is calling the twelve hundred the incidence because it's the bigger number.
Second. Distinguish between incidence and prevalence, using an example to show why the two can move in opposite directions. Pause here to answer.

Define them in parallel: incidence is new cases over a period, prevalence is all cases at one time. Then name the difference. Prevalence also depends on how long people stay cases. So if prevention cuts new cases while a treatment keeps people alive without curing them, incidence falls but prevalence rises. The classic mistake is saying rising prevalence means the condition is spreading.

So, to describe a population's health, use several measures together, ask the five questions of every table, and remember what the averages hide. So for that hundred million, you'd ask for deaths and new cases from cancer and from road injury, as rates, read together, and split by group. And that last point matters most. Next, we'll split the average apart, and ask why giving everyone the same thing often fails to give everyone the same health.
